10. Wo shall now examine the conditions of the last decade at some length
confining our attention to those facta, which have a possible boaring on tho move-
ment of the popalatron.

We have noticed in the last section how the end of the previons decade
(1011—21) witnessed a combmation of adverse crroumstances on an unpreocdented
scale Tho unrest then prevalent was not peculiar to this Province, but had s
world-wide range esen aftermath of the Great War.

The last decade will ever remain memorable for more events than one
Tho Province waa honoured early in the decade by a visit of His Royal Highness
the Prince of Wales, to be soon followed bv the inauguration of an cra of reforms
mtroduced bv the Government of India Act of 1910 Just before the census of
19°] the Punjab had been raised to the status of a Governoc s Province mth a

cabinet consisting of two Members and two Minmtera, of which the latter were
to be selected fram amtongst the elected members of the Legalative Council, which
hod 71 members clected by the people and 20 nominated bx Government The
first session of the Legislative Council wns held on the 2oth January 1021 The
members soon set about their tash in a mght spirt and the Coancil has earned an
enviable repatatian among provinowl legulatures for the dignity of its proceedings
and a high sense of responsibility

The inauguration of the reforms, however did not bring about general ot
matked improvement mn the pobtical artuatron of the country The nonco-
operation movement which had been launched after tho events of 1910 was
pashed on m the first two or three yeara of the decade It included a borcott
of Government and aided schools of foreign cloth and of srvlos m the
Military and Police Departinente The programme also included the extablshing
of Congress commuttees and panchayots m all important towns and villages and
the organiration of a volunteer corps A few national schools were opened
but san rule cloeed down after a brief career

In the ranks of LAilnfatuts disillasionment came asa result of the hardships
which the makayarin (crmgrants) underwent in the autumn of 19°0 when tho
Afghan authorities refused to admit any more of them into thei territory Among
the Sikhs, amtatron of a somewhat different nature was kept alive by the
extremnta who urged the transfer of the control of the Gulden Temple and

the Khalea College at Amntsar a1 the foremost demaml of the community
The body called Shiromam Gurdware Iarbandhak Committee” was formed

The Akah Dal, organised by this Committee, grew to large proportions and began
the sezure by direct action of Sikh shnnes and gurdworas In February 1921 an
attempt was made to seize the Nankana Salub shrine by weight of numbers in
defiance of the Mahant The Mahant’s men opened fire on the mtruders and
about nmety persons were killed and the military had to restore order

The prevalence of crime and unrest at the end of the previous decade was
partly due to demobihzation as well as to political and economic causes In 1922,
however, the situation improved A year later there was further improvement
in the economic conditions, which was reflected in the reduction of mmor crimes
against property The wages maintained a high level while the prices of foodstuffs
went down considerably There was, however httle or no dimmution in the
volume of serious crime and a state of lawlessness, partly the outcome of a
contempt for authonty largely fostered by the Ahah aggressiveness, continued to
render life and property imsecure, particularly m the central Punjab An
increasing boldness and brutality was noticeable in the commission of violent
crimes, exemplified in the savage murder of loyalists im the Jullundur and
Hoshiarpur Districts by the Babbar Ahah gang

The enactment of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act in Julv 19265 and the release
of those, who had been convicted m connection with the Akal: attempt to seize
relimious stitutions by direct action, eased the situation and the agitation which
had disturbed the peace of the Province for several years subsided

In the very first Legislative Council the members began to orgamze communay
themsel es into parties and there was an embryonic grouping of members accord- Gontiet
ing torural and urban interests The other interests, notably communal, were not

The spirit of communal antagonism, fanned by the activities of such movements
as the ‘ shuddix (conversion to Hinduism) and “ tancim,”’ (orgamsationof Muslim
community to combat shuddhz), manifested itself in the serious communal riot at
Multan in 1922, followed m 1926 by even more serious riots in Rawalpindi City
and a neighbouring village Anew and deplorable incident, typical of the period,
occurred at Lahore in 1926, when some hooligans threw a bomb 1n the crowd of
harmless spectators returning after witnessing the celebration of the Dusehra
festival, Jalling many

At the end of the year, Swami Shardhanand, a leader of the “ shuddha”
movement, was murdered in Delhi bya Mushm, and this together with the agitation
arising from excitement consequent on the judgment in the “Rangila Rasul’*
case kept the atmosphere surcharged with mutual distrust andresentment Matters
came to a head when in May 1927 a riot broke out im Lahore, causing several
deaths, followed by communal riots in Multan on the occasion of the Muharram
procession The scene of these activities was transferred to another part of the
Province during ‘the concluding years of the decade, and in 1928 there were serious
nots at Softa m the Gurgaon District and at Mahkpur m the Ambala District as a
result of disputes over cow-slaughter on the occasion of Bakr-Id

«

During 1926 the death-rate at 36 52 per thousand was 5 21 higher than the
average of the previous five years Ramy and cloudy weather m March, April
and May and the consequent continuance of low temperatures and humidity
provided ideal conditions for the spread of plague which was responsible for the
loss of over 108,000 lives There was practically no cholera but a widespread
epidemic of small-pox caused about 17,600 deaths, and the “foyer” death-rate,
owng cluefly to an epidemic of malaria mm the last four months of the year, was
higher than in the previous year and also exceeded the average of the last five
years On the other hand the birth-rate—41 6 per thousand—was also higher
and was exceeded in no other province 1n India except the Central Provinces

The year 1927 was one of the healthiest years m the history of the Punjab,
largely owing to meteorological conditions which were unfavourahle to plague in
the spring and to malaria in the autumn An epidemic of cholera of unusual
intensity, however, prevailed chiefly in Kasur town and tahsil and in the
Ferozepore District which took a toll of 11,286 lves The death-rate of 27 46
per salle was 9 06 per quille less than m 1926 and 5 13 less than the average of the
previous fixe years In fact m only two years in the present century has the
provincial rate beenlower At the same time the birth-rate of 42 3 per melle was
shghtly higher thanin the previous year The infantile mortality rate was also
unusually low, the number of deaths among mfants under one year of age being
1675 per 1,000 Dirths as compared with 203 43 im 1926

In no previous year since vital statistics became available have the people
of the Punjab enjoyed such remathably good health as m the year 1928 Asa
result of the tunely and well distributed rainfall the year 1928 was the healthnest
inthe decade, the birth-rate being 46 30 hich was the Inghest and the death-rate

-94 72, which was the lowest except for 1922 The main cause of the low death-
rate and the high birth-rate was the remarkable freedom from epidemics and more
especially the exceptionally low meidence of plague and malaria The general
healthiness of the year was, however, marred by a very sharp outbreak of cholera
in the Kulu Valley (Kangra District) where 1,746 seizures and 1,164 deaths
occurred, over 70,000 anti-cholera moculations being performed by the Public
Health staff

The distribution of the monsoon was unusual, the dry western districts
of the Province had. abnormal ramfall while 1¢ was in marked defect in the south-
eastern part The monsoon started late and stopped early ‘The ramfall was
particularly heavy during the second fortmght of August, causing heavy floods in
the Jhelum, Chenab and Indus rivers, which resulted m a serious epidemic of
malaria The year 1929 although 1t did not exihbit the remarkable salubrity of the
previous year must be regarded, im spite of certain vicissitudes of chmate, which
occasioned an epidemic of malaria in one Tegion and economic stress in another,

rates except those of Bombay and Central Provinces Apart from the somewhat
severe epidemic of malaria followmg the heavy floods in certam districts the year

18 The general healthmess of the last decade 1s no doubt due to a consider-
able extent to the mauguration of various schemes for the expansion of medical
rehef mm the Provmce In order to attam the ideal of one dispensary for every
100 square miles of territory or for every 30,000 of population the calculations
showed that it would be necessary to open 375 new dispensaries mm rural areas
In 1925 a standard plan for a small and compact dispensary was Jaid down, and
the Government agreed to give a grant of Rs 5,400/- for the construction and
Rs 1,600/- for the equipment of each such dispensary The programme has been
acted upon almost completely durmg the decade, the number of dispensaries
actually opened from 1925 to the end of 1930 bemg 359

The need of efficient arrangements for female medical aid and education
has to some extent been provided for A good number of new female hospitals
and dispensaries was established The Lady Aitchison Hospital, Lahore, and the
Lady Reading Hospital for Women and Children at Simla, have gamed much
popularity durmg the decade The Punjab Medical School for Women, with
which is mcorporated the Women’s Christian College, Ludhiana, is at present the
only mstitution from which women can qualify for appointment as Sub-Assistant
Surgeons During the decade 15 new hospitals for women were opened in various
districts, including the Government Hospital fo. Women and Children at Lahore.
Separate sections for females have been opened m 12 existmg civil hospitals
A notable addition to general hospitals 1s the openmg of the Dental Hospital
at Lahore

19 Some terms that will occur hereafter m this Report may be con- Dennitions

veniently defined at this stage é

& Gultivable Area’? —imcludes land actually under cultivation, fallows
and waste available for cultrvation , such waste does not include areas in which
oultivation 1s forbidden by law or custom, such as reserved forests or common
lands set apart for a specific purpose It does, however, melnde common lands
which can be made available for cultivation by partition even though such parti-
tion has not been effected

“ Gross Cultivated Area ’” —means the area actually sown m any one year
with no deduction for failure of crops, any land sown at both seasons of the year
(8 e, double cropped) bemg counted twice

“ Net Cultivated Area ’? —-means the area sown im any one year, the double
cropped area not bemg counted twice In other words net cultivated area refers
to area of land sown, whilst gross cultivated area refers to the crops sown, to
avoid confusion gross cultivated area 1s referred to generally as the sown area

CO-OPERATIVE MOVEMENT 53

‘may be summed up as a voluntary association of individuals with unrestricted
membership and collectively owned resources formed by small producers (or
artisans, traders, or wage earners) conducted on a democratic basis under joint
management and for mutual service by accumulating the savings of the members
and granting them credit on easy terms by using the jomt responsibility of its
members as a security for loans obtained from outside, surpluses being placed to
reserves In the Punjab an additional element of saving has been mcorporated
by the subscription of shares payable by instalments over a period of ten years
after which they are returnable In the beginning three-quarters of the profits
svere divisible among members as non-returnable shares, and the remammg
quarter was utihzed to form a reserve fund , smce 1918 the principle of indivisible
profits has been. mcorporated in the by-laws Members are encouraged to start
paying m another series of shares, or adopt a system of making compulsury deposits
at regular mtervals on which interest 1s paid

The encouragement of thrift and the ad, ancing of loans only for legitimate
“purposes are the principles which credit societies seek to observe livery village
society has its fixed maximum credit mit beyond which it cannot borrow,

During the last fifty years the population of this Province has msen by a
percentage almost equal to that of India The rate of growth 1s, however, much
smaller than that of England and Wales for the same period, although the latter
lose much of their population by emigration France, which has the smallest
rise of all civilized countries, 1s of course an exception The rise in Sweden is
about the same as in India, and 1¢ would have been much greater but for large
emigration to America The rise in Japan, which 1s due more or less to natural
causes, 13 twice as much asin the Punjab, while the extraordinary rise in the
population of the United States of America 1s nearly four times as much

The increase during the last decade 1s phenomenal, and was certamly
not expected, particularly when it 1s reahsed that the number of deaths
caused by the influenza epidemic of 1918 m British Territory alone was about a
million, out of which the deaths m the reproducing section (aged 15—40) were
417,699 (205,399 males and 212,300 females) The recuperative power of the
Province 1s, however, well-known and the birth-rate after an epidemic or famine
soon recovers its former level, while the death-rate keeps low This has been
ascribed sometimes to the weeding out of the weak elements of society, as evidenced
by the fact that mn 1919 the death-rate fell to 28 3 per mille and m 1922 to 22 per
mille, which 1s the lowest on record since1877 Asregardsthe birth-rate, it had
dropped to 39 6 per mille durmg 1918, the year of the influenza, but rose to 40 3in
the following year and to 42 9 in 1920 as agamst 43 8, the average of the decade.

depend for its cultivation on rainfall Like Jhelum 1t has numerous men m the
Army and many retired soldiers have been allotted colony land Moreover,
its inhabitants are well-known for their enterprise, and many go out to trade
mn distant places and even across the sea and become prosperous On the
high seas men of this district are to be found servimg as lashais on steamers
But for these additional advantages the district would have a great stram on
yésresources The position of Shahpuris unchanged It has the benefit of canal
unigation m three tahsils, while the fourth (Khushab) 1s purely dependent on
rainfall for its crops, but has numerous men serving mthe Army This district
1s, therefore, not faced with any great pressure on its resources Feroze-
pore has benefitted by canal-irrigation from the Sutle) Valley Project
during the last decade, and 1s easily capable of supporting its population, though
the emigration to canal colonies 1s an indication of the increasmg pressure The
bulk of the cultivated area im Mianwali 1s barani (dependent on rainfall), but
the construction of Nammal Dam durmg the previous decade has provided
irrigation to thousands of acres of arid land The cultivated area has enormously
mcreased during the last decade, and the district 13 now regarded as one of the
greatest producers of gram This increase in cultivated area seems to have been
mainly responsible for the rise in population Hissar is at the bottom of the
hst as at last census The greater part of the district 1s sandy and unirigated
Its agricultural resources are therefore, much restricted, but they do not seem
to be subject to any undue pressure of population
From what has been said above it can be safely inferred that Muzaffargarh
and Dera Ghazi Khan inthe south-west and Rohtak, Karnal and Gurgaon in the
south-east are subject to a great pressure on their resources, and any consider-
able rise in their population on future occasions 18 not to be anticipated The
same applies to Sialkot The Hoshiarpur and Jullundur Distnets, which have an
unusually large density of population and which have in the past been able to
support it by means of their agricultural and other resources, are faced with a
grave situation owmg to the receding spring level and dimimshed rainfall
These districts have sent.a very large number of cultivators to the various canal
colonies during the past few decades, and while emigration 1s hkely to be resorted
to as a means of relievmg the increasmmg pressure, the growth of the population
on future occasions will be comparatively restricted The colony districts,
particularly Montgomery, Multan, Sheikhupura and Lyallpur, are likely to
maintain their large mecrease at the next census

55 After having examined the movement in the population of each and
every untt of the Province we may take up the question of accuracy of the
figures In a country, where baseless rumours can cause a mutiny, or a small
meident be so distorted as to lead to most serious riots, 1t 1s only natwal that an
operation like the census should come 1m for :ts share of criticism and suspicion
While in the past all sorts of motives were imputed to Government for taking
a census, the populace is no longer in doubt as to its objects and appreciates 1ts
far-reaching consequences All the same muisapprehensions were not entirely
absent For example, a harmless mstruction about the choice of certam distine-
tive colour for slips, on which entries of certam sects were to be copied to save
a litle labour m abstraction, was construed into an attempt to perpetuate
a sectarian division among the members of the most intellectual communities
m the Province

Under the cirewnstances it 1s not surprising that while some people
complained of omissions in enumeration, some asserted a swelling of the
figures of communities other than ther own by means of bogus entries It has
to be remembered that in the course of an operation of such magmtude as the
census, some omissions are bound to occur But, as remarked by most of the
District officers in their reports, there was a general tendency on the part of the
various communities to have each and every member of theirs enumerated This
is corroborated by the fact that the census population during the last decade
has shown an increase uncqualled m the past There cannot, therefore, have
been many omissions

Coming to the question of artificial swelling of the fgures, we find as al-
ready explained in paragraphs 51 and 52 that the rural population has increased
in all areas as was to be expected from the development of the resources in each
district In this Province as pethaps elsew here too, the pace of merease depends
on the development of material resources For example, with the improvement
in agricultural conditions im an area its population goes up No attempt is
made by the people to keep down their number or to raise ther standard of
living to a level obtaming in the western countries Itis however, undemable
that of late the standard of hving has been 11smg though it has recently been
overshadowed by the prevailmg economic depression Tor instance, an average
person, whether in towns or rural areas, now enjoys many more luxunes and
amenities of life than his forefathers did In most of the districts, particularly
in colony areas, he 1s better fed, better clothed and better housed Earthen
utensils have made room for utensils of biass and other metals, and even glass
and china are no longer a rarity A motor vehicle, which was an object. of
wonder not many years ago, 1s now the commonest means of conveyance in
all parts of the country All the same the fact remains that the standard of
living 1s still susceptible of much improvement and great leeway must be made
before the standard of western countries 1s reached In these circumstances the
phenomenal rise in population cannot be regarded as an unmixed blessmg Be
that as 1 may, the rise m the population of rural areas 1s due to natural mcrease
and migration, and not to any errors in enumeration worth the name

The rise of population in urban areas, which will be discussed fully in the
next Chapter, is to a large extent the mevitable result of the mcreased pros-

Though the net meorease in urban population shown on the fly-leaf to
Imperial Table IV (after omittmg variation due to clusion and exclusion of
towns) gives an idea of the mciease m the urban population which remamed
urban at two consecutive censuses yet it 1s a fact that some of the towns newly
added conta residents of places that were towns in the past but are no longer
so Fo. instance the decaying towns of Kamala Dypalpur, Gogera and Shahpur
ceased to be important because of many of their mhabitants having moved to
the colony towns such as Lyallpur, Sargodha, Montgomery Okara, Gojra, etc
Thus we have a set of people in the Punjab who are chiefly town-dwellers, and
who on migrating from a decaying town settle m anothe: urban area
Some of them would undoubtedly be mcluded m the population of the towns
that are newly added at anv census and will thus contribute to the mcrease in
urban population caused bv the mcelusion of new towns The total mcrease on
this score cannot therefore be rightly excluded from the real merease m urban
population We could thus safely say that the real mcrease in uiban popula-
tion at a census comprises the whole of the merease in the population of the
places classed as towns at that and the preceding censuses and some of the
persons enumerated m the newly-added towns ‘The gross increase in wiban
population durmg the last decade 1s 924,771 or 35 6 per cent over the popula-
tion of 1921, while their net merease 1s 746,213 or 28 9 per cent in respect of
the places treated as towns at both censuses

It 1s appropriate in the beginning to define the five well-known types of
migration

(1) Casual Mrgration—Or the mimor movements between adjacent
villages These affect the returns only when the villages in question happen
to he on opposite sides of the line which divides one district from another

In this type of migration females generally preponderate It arises
largely from the very common practice amongst certain communities, chiofly
Hindus, of taking a wife from another village, and from the fact that young
married women often go to their parents’ home for their first confinement

(2) ZLemporary—Due to journeys on business, visits to places of pil-
grimage and the hke, and the temporary demand for labour when new roads
and railways are under construction

(3) Pertodco —Such as the annual migration which takes place in different
tracts at harvest tue, and the seasonal movements of pastoral nomads

The amount of temporary and periodic migration varies greatly at
different seasons of the year

(4) Sem-Permanent —The natives of one place reside and earn their
living in another, but retam ther connection with ther own homes, where
they leave ther families and to which they return im their old age, and at more
or less regular intervals in the meantime

(5) Permanent —Where overcrowding drives people away or the
superior attractions of some other locality induce people to settle there

REASONS FOR SMALL AMOUNT OF MIGRATION 119

The white squares represent mmigrants to and the shaded squares em1-
grants from this Province The area of the square 1s proportionate to the
number of persons migrating

The reason forthe small amount of migration of all ands was given m
1911 as the proverbial love of the Punjabi for his native land, which made him
content with “ghar ktvadhn, bahw ha sart ” (halfa loaf at homes as good as a whole
away fromit) The real reason however appears to be the one which stands m
the way of urbanization, vz, the dependence of the population on land for
subsistence Food bemg the primary necessity of human hfe keeps people
attached and busy with the land Leisure and off-season are unknown to a
peasant, who has constantly to be near his crop to get a livmg wage out of 1t and
sometimes even less The few moments of leisure, which he can have, are spent
im htigation, of which there 1s no dearth Thus nvgration has no attractions for
the agricultural population except when it 1s calculated to relieve the pressure
on resources by holding out a better agricultural prospect and its attendant
profits in the form of the lease, occupancy or ownership of colony land. A con-
siderable portion of the population consists of artisans and menials, but even
they are supported indirectly by agriculture, and they also do not find any
better substatute for them work to entice them away from their homes

78 Of all the statistics collected at a census those pertaming to age are Introductory
rightly regarded as among the most important A competent authonty* has
remarked that the results of a census operation alone are able to provide precise
notions hoth of the numbers of the people and of \anous important clements
characteristic of the hfe of a nation—data mdispensable to all sound in-
vestigations designed to measure or trace the trend and tendencies contm-
‘buting to national progress ordecay, or to determine the effects or defects
following the application of this or that administrative measure To no other
individual item of the census enquiry ate these remarks more applicable than
to the statistics about age

Unfortunately however the return of age1s probably the most notoriously
ieorrect of all census returns This 1s not only the case wth regard to the age
returns in this country, but even the census of a country hke England and
Wales 1s not free from errors in this respect t

The majority of errors m age returns are fortunately capable of being
corrected, and as errors of practically similar types have been present in the
past, the tabulated figures are not valueless for purposes of comparison Before
explaining the means by which these errors have been elmimated at this census
we will pomt out what the nature of these errorsis The errors are either
deliberate or unintentional In the former case they are due to mis-statement
of age, such as under-statement on the part of unmarried females or elder!
bachelors or widowers The well-known deficiency in this country in the number
of females in the age-group, 15—20, 1s due tothis cause Unintentional errors are

due to looseness of expression, bemg confined mostly to preference for certain
even numbers or numbers ending in zero or five They are also very often

wees 81 In another respect too the age returns at thiscensas differ from those

ar obtained at previons censuses, In all the Indsan Provinces age was recorded
in the past according to the number of yearscompleted The exception wna the
1891 census of this Province when instrnctions were issuod to the enumerators
Tequiting that age should he recorded according to next birthday At the
time of abstraction, however the ages returned were reduced by one year with a
view to obtain « uniform procedure for the whole of India. Thre was really not
heceesary beoanse there wes the usual plomping on certain ages and the persons
enumerated as well aa the enumerators hardly paid any heed to the new instrus-
thon and ages were in all probability returned as Lefore To counteract this
tendency which was recognised by the Actuaries to be due toa tendency on
the part of the public to return age according to the nearest birthday the
Actuanes had always to make due allowance in their computations Mr
Meikle in his report on the 19°1 figures laid particular stress on its recognition.
The new instructions ised mth a view to meet the mtuation and to eccure
some measure of uniformity required age to be recorded according to the nearcat
birthday sux raonths ot more counted asa year and lesa than six months was
tobeontted Thus at last cemas if a person was 20 years and 1] months
old tis age wonld be reconled as 20 years whereas at this census & person

89 Having compared generally the figures of birth and qumquennial
age-groups of the census, we might attempt to deduce the death-rates from
the census population The present census population aged ten years and over
are the survivors of the total population of 1921, the difference between the
two being the total number of deaths during the decade among the population
5 years and over ‘This assumption 1s the same as that adopted by the late
Sir George Hardy in his Actuarial Report of 1901, and gives a death-rate for the
last decade of 30 7 per mille on the mean population of the two censuses The
corresponding death-rate, worked out from the figures of the Pubhe Health
Department, 1s 304 per mille, a figure sufficiently close to the one calculated
above to establish the comparative accuracy of both

After we have determined the death-rate and with its help the amount
of omission in the record, we can find out the number of births with the aid of
actual mcrease in the population, which 1s known to us The birth-rate thus
obtamed 1s 43 9 per mille of the mean population The average birth-rate for
the same period, calculated from the annual rates published by the Public Health
Department, comes to 422 per mille The difference between the calculated
and the published death and birth ratesis 3 and 1 7, respectively, which bears
out the view that the registration of births and deaths has steadily umproved
and is rehable enough, and that the record of births is comparatively less
accurate than that of deaths

characteristic has given rise to a variety of opmions and some foreign critics of
the Indian census have ascribed 1¢ to the incompleteness of returns This
charge has been refuted on several occasions, but 1f any fresh proof was needed
it 1s furnished by the 1931 census of this Province which discloses no marked
variation m the sex proportion in spite of a record intercensal increase m the
population of both sexes

104 This Chapter deals with the marital condition of the population
of the Punjab, or with the numbers of the married unmarnmed and
widowed at different ages andin different localities religions and castes The
divorced persons who had not remarried were meluded among the widowed
Persons living as husband and wife, and recogmsed by custom as married, were
+o be treated as such though they had not gone through the ordinary formalities
connected with marmage The number of such marnages 1s believed however
to be very very small and nothingin comparison to that found in European
countries where some people do not go through any religious ceremony
because they think it is not necessary 1n a state of nature This is evidenced by
the comparatively large number of children regarded by the law m European
countries a3 illegitimate, though born to parents who are man and wife for
all practical purposes The customary marriage im this country 1s confined to
the “ Karews’’ known locally by different names, which 1s the taking into
wedlock of the widow of a deceased brother or some other near relative, such as
@ first cousin

The Punjab Census Report of 1911 (p 275) deals at length with the
customs and ceremonies, performed at the time of marriage among different
communities and castes It 1s unnecessary to repeat them here except
to mention that marriage is believed by o great majority of the people to be
mote or less a sacrament or 4 religious duty Divorce 1s unknown to the Hindu
law, as also among Sikhs and Jams, and even among Muslims though 1 18
permissible the cases of divorce are few and far hetween and the compuation
of separate figures 1s uncalled for,

In the case of different religions the proportion of marriageable males per

3.062 among Mushms and 3,142 among Christians

The figures obtained as a result of this enquiry are given m Imperial
Table IX, Parts I and II It may be remarked that the figures of mfirmities

especially leprosy or msanity among females, 1s seldom given out The only

Jt may be mentioned that the compilation of the occupations table
ig one of the most difficult of all the consus undertakings An elaborate revised
index showing the classification of all occupations returned at former censuses

Commussioner for India supplied another mdex It will, however, be admitted
that no mdex could be exhaustive enough adequately to provide for the diver-
sity of the returns that were met with at the time of sorting The entries not
only depend on the fancy of the persons questioned but also on that of the
enumerator However complete the tramimg, to which the huge army of enume-
rators1s subjected, 1618 not possible to suppress individual freaks altogether
As a result some of the most amusmg occupations were recorded In some
cases the columns of occupation contamed such entries as ‘ school-boy ’ and
‘godha,’ a most unusual term which meant an infant in arms and gave any
amount of trouble to the establishmient of the soiting office to deorpher Even
the wives of British Army officers were found to have returned the occupation

cases the entry about political prisoners or Europeans in the column of occu-
pation was ‘ refuses to disclose further particulais’ Sometimes the occupation
recorded was ‘ guest,’ and a new departure made at this census was the entry
of ‘ Congress,’ ‘ National Worker,’ ‘ Volunteer,’ or ‘Bande Matram’ as the
occupation of an earner These cases are quoted to give an idea of the entnes
which are met with and which are more or less unavoidable The total
number of such entries 1s however small, and even rf some returns have

been wrongly recorded the final results of the census could not be materially

Trade in textiles has shown a faily big increase This order moludes
the “ Bazaz”’ (cloth merchant), who has plied a profitable trade during the
‘prosperous years of the last decade

This industry appears to have declmed, but the trade in skins which 1s
the chief 1tem in, this order shows an increase of 19 4 per cent

There is an increase in the trade mn wood, pottery, bricks and tiles, but
the trade in chemical products hke the industry shows adecline The compara~
tively small trade m metals seems to be growing

Hotels, cafes and restaurants show a big increase indicative of a new
social development Formerly taking refreshments and meals at hotels and
testaurants was almost unknown, but with the increased facilities of travelling
the habit 1s spreading and promises to play a prominent part in the social hfe
Thus in a place hke Lahore the house-wife could in many cases be considerably
relieved of her ordmary duties and will find more leisure for handicrafts such as
embroidery, knitting and spinning

There 1s a decrease in this order due almost entirely to the transfer of

ties for daily use, from sugar candy to medicinal herbs, from paraffin oil to rat
‘poisons, and what not

This order deals with the “ besatz ” nar excellence, and shows an increase
nearly proportionate to the general rise in the total population

SECTION 4.—EDUC.¢TED UNEMPLOYMENT.

- 173 On the next page appears Table XIT of this census the only
Imperial Table tobe printed m this part of the Volume The figures con-
tamed im it are abstracted from special schedules, filled up by those whose
minimum educational qualification was Matriculation standard, and who were
unemployed or dissatisfied with their jobs and wishful for employment These
schedules were distributed by the enumerators in the course of the prelimu-
nary enumeration and collected when they went round ther blocks on the
final census night The fillmg-uwp of the schedules was voluntary, and the
response was extremely meagre The figures in the table consequently do not at
all represent the extent of the educated unemployment It 1s difficult to draw
definite conclusions from the figures, but it may be safely remarked that the
greatest unemployment exists among the matriculates, aged between 20 and
24 years The next highest figuresare among the Arts graduates of the same
age The number among other classes is very small Those remarks relate
to Part II of the Table The only indication of the figures in Part I 18 that

number of literate males above the age of 20 aé this census, He estimated an
annual morense of 50 000 as « result of the attainment of fresh literacy by boys
atachool. To the probable survivors of these he added the probable survivors of
the Iterates of 1021 ond thus obtained the figure of 814808 as the total
number of malo Irterates over 20 m Brrish Terntory at the census. His
surmise about the number of hterates, turned out by the schools during the
last decade, has proved to be fairly correct, but what he seems to have over
looked 1s that a great majonty of these boys would be still below 20 in

LITERACY IN ENGLISH 259

The table also shows how certain castes, such as Aggarwal, Khatri and Arora,
have stood out at both the censuses with a prominently high percentage of
literacy The figures of these castes would compare favourably even with
those of Europeans, Anglo-Indians or Zoroastrians, uf the comparison were
confined to persons between the ages of 15 and 40 Brahmans, Sayads and
Sheikhs seem to be literate in famwly large numbers, and to a lesser extent
Pathans and Kashmiris The agricultural castes are, of course, very back-
ward, but Rajputs, who receive large accretions from the well-to-do and educa-
ted members of lower castes, and Sainis are proportionately better educated,
while of the others Kambohs, "Jats, Awans and Arains are almost on the same
level The Ahirs, Guyjars and Meos are m the background, though the two
last-named have made much progress during the last decade As regards
the artisan castes, such as Lohar and Tarkhan, there 1s not much to choose be-
tween them and their agriculturist neighbours Jat and Aram, while the Sunar
(goldsmith) 1s comparatively much better off Of the village menials, Kumhar,
Moc, Telr, Machh: and Dhob: are still backward, and the criminal tribes under
State supervision have drawn level with them, the Pakhiwara actually claiming
a higher proportion of literacy The depressed classes, namely, Dagi and Koh,
Chamar and Chuhra, and their Muslim counterparts, Mochi and Mussalh, are
the most backward of all

edition 15 “the hands of readers in Lahore before sunrise, bemg distributed

Tho most notable feature of the present consus fiom the standpoint of A“ New”
return of religion has beon the adoption of the term ‘ Ad-Dharmi’ by numerous Religion.
Chamars and Chuhras and other untouchables At previous censuses Chuhras,
unless thoy returned some recognised religion, were always included among
Hindus In this respect tho instructions for the return of religion at the present
consus were the same as n1921, wz, ‘All Chuhras, who are not Muslims or
Christians, and who do not return any other religion, should be returned as
Hindus The same iule applies to members of other depressed classes who
have no tribal religion ” Thus under the structions if a Chuhra refused to be
recorded as 2 Hindu he was to be so recorded in case he failed to return any
other rehgion An addition was, however, made to the mstructions by the
insertion of the clauso —‘‘ Persons returning themselves as Ad-Dharnus should
be recorded as such’? The Punjab Ad-Dharm Mandal had petitioned the
Punjab Government before the census operations started m 1930, representing
that the depressed classes should be permitted to return Ad-Dharm as
their religion at tho time of the consus as they were the aborigines of India and
while the Hindus kept thom at a respectable distance they did not believe mn
the Hindu religion The President of the Punjab Ad-Dharm Mandal was
informed that a clause was being provided in the Census Code requiring that
persons returning their religion as Ad-Dhaim would be recorded as suoh
Ad-Dharm literally means original or ancient religion

The main conclusion 1s that the varying strength of the population re-
turned as Hindu or Sikh in the Punjab States 1s due to social causes that are
at work in that section of the population, from which both Hindus and Sikhs.
are drawn The Akal: movement during the last decade 1s mamly responsible
for numerous persons being returned as Sikhs mstead of Hindus Such persons
for the most part comprise members of dopressed classes, agriculturists and
artisans in rural areas, who obviously consider that they gam in status as soon
as they cease to be Hindus and become Sikhs

An indication of this 1s furmshed by the variation in the numerical
strength of many occupational castes and certain tribes, such as Jat, Saim,
Rajput and Arora, whose members are returning themselves in increasingly
large numbers as Sikhs instead of Hindus, particularly in the districts and
states of the central Punjab There are certain other tribes, such as Chuhra
and Chamar, who chafing under the label of untouchabihty prefer Sikhism to

Below are given some quotations from the Census Reports of the past,
which graphically desortbe certain phases of the Sikh community bearing on
the rise and fall m its population at various periods

The following extracts appear at page 140 of the Punjab Census Report
of 1881 —

In 1853 Sir Richard Templo wrote, as Secrotary to the Government —

“ The Sikh faith and ecclesiastical polity 1s rapidly going whore the Sikh political ascendancy has already
gone Of tho two elements in the old Khalsa, namely, the followers af Nanak the first prophot, and the followers
of Gurn Gobind, the second great religious leader, the former will hold ther » and the latter will lose
it The Sikhs of Nanak, a comparatively small body of peaceful habits and old family, will perhaps olmg to
the faith of ther fathers but the Sikhs of Gobind who are of more recent origin, who are more specially styled
the Singhs or Lions, and who embraced the faith as bemg the religion of warfare and conquest, no longer regard
the Khalsa now that tho prestige has departed from it These men jomed in thousands, and they now d
m equal number ‘They rejoin the ranks of Hinduism whence they orgimally came and they bring up their
children as Hindus ‘The sacred tank at Ammtsar 1s less thronged than formerly, and the attendance at the
annual festival is dummishing yearly Tho imtintory ceremony for adult persons 18 now rarely performed.”

In the Admmmistration Report of 1856-57 the same writer says after
speaking of the small number of Sikh recruits that offered themselves till the
fall of Delhi proclaimed our triumph

** Sikhism itself, too, which had Previously fallen off so much, seems ngain to be slightly on the increase.
Dumng the past year the baptismal mutiations at the Amritsar temple have been more numerous than during
the preceding year Sikhism is not dormant”

And Colonel MacMahon, Commissioner of Amritsar, writes as follows in
his Census Report —

“The large decrease in the number of Sikhs since 1868 1s not surprsing Sikhs declme in number, In
years of peace There was a serious decline, I believe, after the conquest of the Punjab down to 1857, when
the demand for Sikhs for our army d the mutiny for a time gave a great stimulus to the growth of Sikhism,
Tho idea prevails, not only with the officers of native regiments, but also among the classes from which Sikh
converts are obtamed, that Sikhs made better soldiers than Punjabi Hindus, and Hence whenever tho warlike
gpirit revives, Sikhism in this part of the Punjab also revives All tho members of the same family do not always
become Sikhs and those who have acquired a taste for the soothing influence of tobacco abstata from talung
the pakul Hence in tames of peace there is a tendenoy for Sikhism to dechne.”

“ Thero is reason to believe that the marked preference shown for Sikhs in many branches of Government.
service, the hardy nature of the castes from which they are mamly drawn, and the recent extension of a kmd
of patriotic antiquarianism among the more educated of them, has not been without ita influence in strengthening
their power and preventing the disruption of the Sikh community which one has so often seen predicted ”

marked advance sinoe 1891, possibly at the expense of Hinduism, for the Hindus only show an increase of
24 per cent’

The phenomenal increase continued even durmg the very unhealthy
decade preceding the census of 1911, when the total population of the Pro-
vince showed an actual decrease After remarking about the absence of sepa-
rate vital record for Sikhs, the 1911 Report with regard to the mcrease im their
number said —

“Nevertheless tho rate of increase 1s much too Ingh for the natural development of
the umhygienic conditions which prevauled during the decade. The gain ccoms to have ocala dee
accretions from the Hindus It has not been possible to ascertain the number of people who have taken the pakul

312 Numerous persons at this census abstamed from returning a caste,
and many of them deliberately It 1s quite possible that some of the omissions
im the column of caste were accidental, having creptin during one of the several
stages of the census operations The number of Brahmamic Hindus, who did
not return a caste, is negligible, bemg 4,419 males and 2,397 females out of a total
population of over eight milhons, and Caste would thus seem to have, as ever,
1ts grip onthe population In the case of 50 per cent of the followers of Vedic
Dharm, numbermg 341,390 persons (194,355 males and 147,035 females), the
entry 1n the caste column was Arya, which 1s the equivalent of ‘ no caste’ entry
in the case of Brahmanic Hindus (mainly Sanatanists) The main figures of
‘no caste’ entry among Brahmanic Hindus relate to Amritsar (1,626), Gujrat
(1,191), Gujranwala (914) and Gurdaspur (685) It 1s rather surprising that
Lahore, claiming as 1t does a large number of people with advanced views, has
had very few such entries Some‘ no caste’ entries, practically all relating to
females, in places hike Suket and Jhelum, seem to be due to a statistical
error, as also those relating to an excessive number of malesin Amritsar On
the whole, it can safely be said that very few of the Brahmanic Hindus have
refrained from returning their caste although there was a considerable propaganda
against the return of caste, particularly that emanating from the Jat Pat Torak
Mandal My conclusionis that people prefer to return a higher caste to return-
ing no caste, and that the caste system has still a great hold on them.

APPENDIX I
VITAL STATISTICS

The system of registermg vital statistics im the British Districts 1s
as follows In the rural circles, births and deaths ‘are reported by village
chaukidars (watchmen) who are provided with two books, one for births and
the other for deaths, in which entries are made, on the chauladar’s report, by
a resident of the village who can read and write, and the lambardars (village
headmen) of each village are responsible that these entries are duly made The
chaukidars take their books with them to the Thana (police station) at their
fortmghtly visits and from these books and from oral enquiries made from
chauladars, the Police Auharrirs compile the fuller registers which they mam-
tan. Fortnightly returns are submitted, through the Superintendent of
Police, to the Civil Surgeon The Civil Surgeon forwards fortnightly, monthly
and annual returns, compiled from the Police returns, to the Director of Public
Health, Punjab YTrom the returns so received, monthly and annual returns
are prepared in the office of the Director of Public Health, Punjab The Police
Muharrirs recerve a small monthly allowance m all cases in which the work
1s done satisfactorily In Municipal towns, when a birth or death occurs in any
household, the head of the household makes a report withm three days of the
occurrence or causes a report to be made orally or upon a form provided by the
Committee Iffor any reason he1s unable todo so, the report 1s made by an
adult member of his family, or failing any such, by an adult male servant,

or 1n the case of births, by the midwife employed in the accouchement If9 (

birth or death occursin a household in which there 1s no grown up male member,
thereport 1s made by the sweeper of the mohalla (street or lane) The mohalla-
dar (a responsible resident of the mohalla) and the sweeper are jomtly and
severally responsible that there is no omission In most Municipalities, rules
or bye-laws have been adopted under the Municipal Act, regarding the proper
registration of births and deaths In towns where no special bye-laws for the
registration ot vital statistics have been prescribed by the Municipal Committee,
but where the watch and ward 1s done by the Municipal Police the constable
of each beat reports all deaths occurring init The police are assisted by the
sweepers of the mohallas, who supply the formation regarding births Birth
and death registers are kept at Municipal Registry Offices, and weekly returns
compiled from the registers are forwarded to Civil Surgeons for incorporation
in therr district weekly returns A weekly return showing the births and deaths
registered im all Municipal towns with a population often thousand and upwards

each, and a monthly return showing the births and deaths registered in all
districts, are published in the Punjab Government Gazette

The accuracy of the registers mamtained by the Police and Munnecipali-
ties 18 tested by the Director of Public Health, Punjab, and Assistant Directo
of Public Health and District Medical Officers of Health, Civil Sur eo ..
Superintendents and Assistant Supermtendents of Police, Tahsildars ee "
Tahsildars, Kanungos, Supermtendents of Vaccination and Vacemators “All
omissions of births and deaths are supplied im the registers after verification

by the Civil Surgeons, and
byt geons, and the District Officers are asked to punish the defaul-
